q: Explain the difference between Normandy and Basque cider in three dimensions.

q: What would you pour with a cheese course if the guest does not drink wine?
accept: gueuze saison sweet cider sake trappist
tart beer or cider
ans: A gueuze or saison for washed rinds and hard cheeses, an off-dry cider for bloomy, or a barley wine for blue — acid and effervescence do the work sugar and tannin would

q: Compare a Flanders red such as Rodenbach with a lambic: souring organisms, vessel, timescale and the resulting acid profile.
accept: lambic is spontaneous in a coolship and old barrels giving lactic brett character flanders red is pitched and foeder aged with acetic oxidation
lambic wild lactic and dry flanders red oxidative acetic and blended young into old
spontaneous fermentation and bottle blending versus mixed culture in oak foeders for two years
ans: Lambic is spontaneously inoculated: unhopped-tasting, aged-hop wort is cooled overnight in an open coolship, picking up the Senne valley air and, more importantly, the brewery's own resident house flora, then racked to neutral old barrels where an ordered succession plays out over one to three years — Enterobacteria first, then Saccharomyces, then Pediococcus producing lactic acid, then Brettanomyces consuming long-chain dextrins and generating the barnyard, citrus-peel and hay character. The result is highly attenuated, bone dry, lactic and funky, with very little acetic sharpness because the barrels are full and oxygen ingress is low. Gueuze is a blend of young and old lambic refermented in bottle. Flanders red is pitched, not spontaneous: a Vienna and caramel malt beer, deep amber-red from the malt rather than from fruit, fermented with a mixed culture and then matured 18 months to two years in large upright oak foeders, where Lactobacillus and Brettanomyces work alongside deliberate slow oxygen ingress. That oxidative environment builds acetic acid and ethyl acetate on top of the lactic acidity, giving the balsamic, sour-cherry, vinegary profile. The house then blends aged beer back into young for balance — Rodenbach's flagship is roughly a quarter two-year foeder beer, Grand Cru about two-thirds — and most commercial bottlings are sweetened or blended down for the market. In short: lambic tastes of wild fermentation, Flanders red tastes of oxidative barrel age. One is Brussels' answer to Champagne, the other Flanders' answer to red Burgundy.
exp: Sour beer is not one category, and knowing which acid you are selling is the somm's job: lactic acidity behaves at table like a high-acid white, while the acetic and ethyl acetate lift of a Flanders red behaves like a sherry-vinegar seasoning and will fight a delicate dish. Cite the Rodenbach blend ratios and you have shown you understand that solera-style blending, not spontaneity, is the defining technique here.

q: What must a brewery satisfy to carry the Authentic Trappist Product hexagon, and which breweries hold it today?
accept: brewed inside the monastery walls under monastic supervision with income supporting the community and charity
the three international trappist association criteria on location supervision and non commercial purpose
authentic trappist product certifies governance not style five belgian breweries plus la trappe zundert engelszell tre fontane mount st bernard and cardena
ans: Three conditions set by the International Trappist Association, founded in 1997: the beer must be brewed within the walls of a Trappist monastery; it must be brewed by or under the direct supervision of the monastic community; and the brewery must be subordinate to the monastery, run without a profit motive, with income covering the community's needs and the remainder going to charity and social work. It is a governance mark, not a style and not a quality guarantee — it says nothing about how the beer tastes. Current holders: Chimay, Orval, Rochefort, Westmalle and Westvleteren in Belgium; La Trappe (Koningshoeven) and Zundert in the Netherlands; Engelszell in Austria; Tre Fontane in Italy; Mount St Bernard's Tynt Meadow in England; and Cardena in Spain — around ten or eleven, and the number moves. Achel lost the label in 2021 when its last monks left, and Spencer in the United States ceased brewing in 2022. 'Abbey beer' is an entirely separate commercial category: beers using a monastery's name under licence, or carrying the Belgian Brewers' certified Abbey Beer logo, brewed by ordinary commercial breweries anywhere.
exp: The hexagon is regularly mis-sold to guests as a quality tier. Point out that Orval and Westmalle Tripel share nothing stylistically, that the ATP also covers cheese, bread and cosmetics, and that plenty of secular abbey beers outdrink Trappists. Knowing that the roster changes — and why Achel and Spencer left it — is what distinguishes current knowledge from a memorised list.

q: Order a beer in Plzen like a Czech: explain the Balling categories, tank beer, and the three pours.
accept: degrees balling is original gravity vycepni lezak and special tankove pivo is unpasteurised hladinka snyt and mliko
balling measures original gravity rather than alcohol a lezak is eleven or twelve degrees
the three pours are hladinka snyt and mliko and tank beer is unpasteurised cellar tank beer
ans: Czech beer is classified by original gravity in degrees Balling, essentially identical to Plato. Vycepni is the everyday draught at about 8-10 degrees; lezak, the lager proper, sits at 11-12 — Pilsner Urquell is 11.8, about 4.4% abv; special is 13 and above. The number is gravity rather than alcohol, and assuming a 'twelve' means 12% is the standard foreigner's error. Tankove pivo is unpasteurised, unfiltered or lightly filtered beer delivered by tanker and held in cellar tanks under an air-free gas envelope, drunk within days: softer, rounder, more bread and hop, and the single largest quality variable in a Czech pub. The pours come off a side-pull tap with a fine screen. Hladinka is the standard: clear beer under roughly three fingers of dense, wet, creamy foam. Snyt is a short measure — less beer, the same deep head — for when you want a small beer in a full-size glass. Mliko, 'milk', is a glass poured entirely to foam: sweet, creamy, low in bitterness because the bitter compounds partition differently, and drunk immediately as a chaser rather than sipped.
exp: Two teachable points. First, degrees Balling are gravity — a 12-degree lezak lands near 5% abv, and the number describes the wort you started from, which is why it also predicts body. Second, the foam is functional rather than a short measure: a thick wet head protects the beer from oxidation and carries aroma, and a Czech pub serving flat, foamless beer has made a mistake by their standards rather than by yours.

q: Which beers reward cellaring and which do not, and what chemistry decides it?
accept: hoppy and pale beers fade while high gravity dark and bottle conditioned sour beers improve
trans-2-nonenal cardboard oxidation drives staling so store cold dark and upright
age strong dark styles and lambic drink ipa and pilsner as fresh as possible
ans: The default direction of beer with age is downward. Oxygen picked up at packaging drives lipid and melanoidin oxidation toward trans-2-nonenal, the wet-cardboard marker, perceptible at fractions of a part per billion; hop aroma volatiles blow off within weeks to a few months; iso-alpha acids degrade, so bitterness fades and the beer flabbies out; and every one of those reactions roughly doubles in rate for each 10C, which means a warm warehouse or a summer container ages a beer faster than years in a cold cellar. That condemns exactly the beers people cellar by mistake: hoppy pale ales and IPAs, which should be drunk as close to packaging as you can buy them, and delicate pale lagers and Pilsners, where there is nothing to hide behind. What genuinely improves: high-gravity, high-alcohol styles where oxidation reads as sherried, dried-fruit complexity rather than fault — barley wine, imperial stout, doppelbock and eisbock, Belgian quadrupel; anything with living secondary flora that keeps working — lambic and gueuze, Orval with its Brettanomyces, bottle-conditioned saison; and barrel-aged sours, which are already built out of controlled oxidation. Storage: cold, dark, stable; bottle-conditioned beer upright so the yeast forms a compact plug and the crown seal stays dry rather than soaking. And on a list, print the packaging date on the fresh styles and the vintage on the ageable ones — they are two different products and should be sold as such.
exp: Name the fault correctly and you fix the right thing: cardboard and sherry are oxidation and heat, skunk is light exposure, and butterscotch is unfinished fermentation. Different causes, different people to blame. The 10C doubling rule is the most useful single fact here — it is why refrigerated distribution matters more to a hoppy beer than the brewer's recipe does.

accept: climens la tour blanche lafaurie-peyraguey clos haut-peyraguey rayne-vigneau rieussec suduiraut coutet guiraud rabaud-promis sigalas-rabaud
climens suduiraut coutet
rieussec
ans: Climens, La Tour Blanche, Lafaurie-Peyraguey, Clos Haut-Peyraguey, Rayne-Vigneau, Rieussec, Suduiraut, Coutet, Guiraud, Rabaud-Promis, Sigalas-Rabaud
exp: Eleven premiers today — but the 1855 list itself named nine; Peyraguey was later divided into Lafaurie-Peyraguey and Clos Haut-Peyraguey, and Rabaud into Rabaud-Promis and Sigalas-Rabaud. Climens rules Barsac.

q: Give the technical term and mechanism of Bordeaux's June 'mildiou' nemesis versus 'oïdium'.
accept: downy mildew plasmopara vs powdery erysiphe
peronospora downy oidium powdery
ans: Mildiou = downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola, wet-season, oily spots, Bordeaux-mixture target); oïdium = powdery mildew (Erysiphe necator, dry-tolerant, sulfur target)
exp: Both American imports that rewrote European spray calendars before phylloxera finished the job.
